title: Earth's churning mantle may have created the Great Unconformity
gist: A Nature study by Santosh Dhungana and Nicolas Flament uses six mantle-convection simulations over 1 billion years to argue the Great Unconformity formed when long mantle-driven uplift of Laurentia coincided with Snowball Earth glacial erosion, then Cambrian subsidence buried it. Pure earth-science piece with no direct market angle.

insights.claim: Simulations suggest slow mantle convection pushed continents like Laurentia up for hundreds of millions of years, letting glaciers erode them before they sank and were buried by Cambrian sediments.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Scientific result; no direct investment relevance.

insights.claim: Five of six models showed Laurentia experiencing long uplift followed by Cambrian sinking, while northern Europe and North China showed the pattern in four.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko

insights.claim: Mantle uplift alone was too gentle to create the Great Unconformity; coinciding Snowball Earth glaciation, roughly 10 times more erosive than rivers, supplied the missing erosion.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Illustrates coincidence of independent processes explaining rare outcomes.
insights.quote: They’re not coupled. They just happen to coincide in time.

insights.claim: Flament acknowledges model uncertainty: ancient continental longitudes are unknown and some continents may be in the wrong hemisphere, while ancient ocean floor had to be invented.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Caveat on reliability of deep-time reconstructions.
insights.quote: It’s possible that some continents may be in the wrong hemisphere

insights.claim: North America and Eurasia show one long rise and fall, the ideal recipe for the unconformity, whereas South America and Australia had two cycles, making the gap harder to see.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Explains geographic variation of the feature.

insights.claim: Erosion that carved the Great Unconformity may have fertilized oceans with calcium before the Cambrian explosion, though Flament says the mantle was only one contributing force.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Speculative link between geology and the evolution of skeletons and shells.
insights.quote: I think it would be misleading to say the mantle set the pace here.
